```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(tidyverse)  
library(lubridate)   
library(janitor)     
```

# 1. Introduction

This project analyzes the dataset **"Reporte Hurto por Modalidades Policía
Nacional"** (Theft Report by Modalities - National Police), published on
Colombia's Open Data portal (https://www.datos.gov.co), provided by the
Dirección General de la Policía Nacional - DIPON. The dataset contains
individual theft case records in Colombia (modalities such as theft from
persons, residences, vehicles, businesses, motorcycles, livestock theft
"abigeato", financial institutions, and highway robbery "piratería"), with
variables for department, municipality, DANE code, weapon or means used,
date of the incident, victim's gender and age group, type of theft, and
number of cases.

**Research questions:**

1. How has the number of thefts in Colombia evolved year by year? Is there a
   clear trend (increase, decrease, or stability)?
2. Is there seasonality in thefts? Are there months of the year where
   consistently more cases are reported?

# 2. Loading and Initial Exploration of the Data

```{r load-data}

hurtos <- read_csv("hurtos.csv",
                    locale = locale(encoding = "UTF-8"))


glimpse(hurtos)
```

```{r clean-names}

hurtos <- hurtos %>% clean_names()
names(hurtos)
```

```{r initial-summary}
summary(hurtos)


table(hurtos$tipo_de_hurto)


range(hurtos$fecha_hecho)
```

# 3. Data Cleaning

```{r clean-dates}
hurtos <- hurtos %>%
  mutate(
    fecha_hecho = dmy(fecha_hecho),     
    year = year(fecha_hecho),
    month = month(fecha_hecho)
  )


sum(is.na(hurtos$fecha_hecho))


table(hurtos$year)
```

The dataset covers from January 2010 to March 2026. This
means **2010 and 2026 are likely NOT complete years**, which would distort
the trend and the monthly comparison. For this reason, for the trend and
seasonality analysis we will only use complete years (2011-2025). Adjust this
range based on what you see in the table above.

```{r filter-complete-years}
hurtos_complete <- hurtos %>%
  filter(year >= 2011, year <= 2025)
```

# 4. General Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

Before answering the main research questions, let's look at the overall
picture of the dataset.

```{r eda-theft-type}
hurtos_complete %>%
  group_by(tipo_de_hurto) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(cantidad, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  arrange(desc(total)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(tipo_de_hurto, total), y = total)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Total cases by theft type (2011-2025)",
       x = "Theft type", y = "Total cases") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Note on this dataset:** in this particular file, the majority of
records correspond to **HURTO ABIGEATO** (livestock theft)  about 85% of
all rows (37,548 out of 44,169)  while **HURTO PIRATERÍA TERRESTRE** (highway
robbery, 4,841 cases) and **HURTO ENTIDADES FINANCIERAS** (theft from
financial institutions, 1,780 cases) make up the rest. Keep this in mind when
interpreting the results below: the overall patterns are heavily driven by
livestock theft.

```{r eda-departments}
hurtos_complete %>%
  group_by(departamento) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(cantidad, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  arrange(desc(total)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(departamento, total), y = total)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 10 departments with the most thefts (2011-2025)",
       x = "Department", y = "Total cases") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r eda-gender}
hurtos_complete %>%
  filter(genero %in% c("MASCULINO", "FEMENINO")) %>%
  group_by(genero) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(cantidad, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = genero, y = total, fill = genero)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Total thefts by victim gender (2011-2025)",
       x = "Gender", y = "Total cases") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# 5. Research Question 1: Annual Evolution of Thefts

```{r q1-table}
hurtos_annual <- hurtos_complete %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(cantidad, na.rm = TRUE))

hurtos_annual
```

```{r q1-plot}
ggplot(hurtos_annual, aes(x = year, y = total)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Annual evolution of thefts in Colombia (2011-2025)",
       x = "Year", y = "Total reported cases") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r q1-regression}
trend_model <- lm(total ~ year, data = hurtos_annual)
summary(trend_model)
```

**How to interpret this result:**

- The coefficient for `year` indicates how much the total number of thefts
  changes (on average) for each additional year. If positive, the trend is
  increasing; if negative, decreasing.
- The **p-value** associated with that coefficient tells you whether this
  trend is statistically significant (usually considered significant if
  p < 0.05).
- The **R-squared** indicates what proportion of the year-to-year variation
  is explained by a simple linear trend.

**Results for this dataset:** the annual totals rise from 1,884 cases in
2011 to a peak of 5,741 cases in 2017, and then decline steadily to 957 cases
in 2025. The regression coefficient for `year` is -66.13 with p = 0.379 (not
significant), and R-squared is only 0.06. This low fit is expected: the data
does **not** follow a straight line — it rises for several years and then
falls, forming a peak around 2017. A simple linear trend is therefore not the
right way to describe this pattern; a more accurate description is "rise then
decline," with the overall direction since 2017 being a sustained decrease.

# 6. Research Question 2: Seasonality

## 6.1 Total Thefts by Month (All Years Combined)

```{r q2-monthly}
hurtos_monthly <- hurtos_complete %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(cantidad, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(hurtos_monthly, aes(x = factor(month), y = total)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange") +
  labs(title = "Total thefts by month (2011-2025, all years combined)",
       x = "Month (1 = January, 12 = December)", y = "Total cases") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 6.2 Monthly Distribution Across Years (Boxplot)

```{r q2-boxplot}
hurtos_month_year <- hurtos_complete %>%
  group_by(year, month) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(cantidad, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(hurtos_month_year, aes(x = factor(month), y = total)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of monthly thefts across years (2011-2025)",
       x = "Month (1 = January, 12 = December)", y = "Total cases") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 6.3 Statistical Test: Does the Month Influence the Total Number of Thefts?

```{r q2-anova}
month_anova <- aov(total ~ factor(month), data = hurtos_month_year)
summary(month_anova)
```

**How to interpret this result:**

- The ANOVA compares the total number of thefts across the 12 months (using
  each year-month combination as one observation).
- If the **p-value** is below 0.05, there is evidence that at least one
  month has a significantly different average than the others, i.e.,
  evidence of seasonality.
- Combine this result with the bar chart (6.1) to identify *which* months
  tend to have more or fewer cases (for example, does December stand out?).

**Results for this dataset:** the ANOVA gives F = 0.444 and p = 0.934, which
is far from significant — there is no statistical evidence that the month of
the year affects the total number of thefts. Looking at the bar chart, January
has the highest total (~4,100 cases) and October-December are slightly lower
(~3,200 cases), but this difference is small relative to the year-to-year
variability shown in the boxplot, which is why it does not reach statistical
significance.

# 7. Conclusions

**Annual trend:** the number of reported thefts did not follow a simple
increasing or decreasing trend over 2011-2025. Instead, cases rose from 2011
through a peak in 2017 (5,741 cases), and have declined steadily every year
since, reaching 957 cases in 2025 — the lowest value in the series. The
overall linear regression was not statistically significant (p = 0.379,
$R^2$ = 0.06), confirming that a straight-line trend does not adequately describe
this rise-then-fall pattern.

**Seasonality:** there is no statistically significant evidence of
seasonality (ANOVA p = 0.934). While January shows a slightly higher total
than other months, the difference is small compared to the variability
between years, so it cannot be considered a reliable seasonal pattern.

**Context:** these results are heavily influenced by **HURTO ABIGEATO**
(livestock theft), which represents about 85% of all records in this dataset.
This also helps explain why the departments with the most cases (Cundinamarca,
Cesar, Tolima, Antioquia, Meta, etc.) are largely rural/agricultural regions,
and why the majority of victims are male (~31,000 vs ~7,000 female) —
consistent with patterns of livestock ownership in Colombia.

**Limitations:** the data come from official police reports and may not
capture unreported cases. The years 2010 and 2026 were excluded from the
analysis because they were incomplete. Additionally, since this dataset only
contains three theft modalities (livestock, financial institutions, and
highway robbery), these conclusions apply specifically to these types of
theft and should not be generalized to all forms of theft in Colombia (e.g.,
theft from persons or residences, which are reported in separate datasets).
